items.question: Examine the market-control and military reforms of Alauddin Khalji. Why were they interlinked, and how far did they succeed?
items.modelAnswer:
Alauddin Khalji (1296–1316) was the first Sultan of Delhi to build a **coercive but coherent economic-military state**, and his **market (price-control) reforms** and **military reforms** were two halves of a single design. His central problem was how to maintain a **large standing army** — needed to repel repeated **Mongol invasions** and to finance Deccan expansion — without exhausting the treasury.

His solution was to make soldiering cheap by **fixing low prices for essential commodities**. He created separate controlled markets in Delhi — the grain **mandi**, the cloth-and-general market **Sarai Adl**, and a market for horses, slaves and cattle — each under a superintendent, the **Shahna-i-Mandi**. A dedicated department, the **Diwan-i-Riyasat**, registered every merchant, while the **Barid** (official reporter) and **munhiyans** (secret spies) sent the Sultan daily reports, and hoarding was severely punished. Grain was procured through a state levy and stored, so prices held even in scarcity.

On the **military side**, he was the first to keep a **large permanent army paid in cash** from the treasury, and to enforce the **Dagh** (branding of horses) and **Chehra** (a written descriptive roll of each soldier) system to stop muster fraud. Because prices were low, fixed cash salaries stretched far — so the market reforms were what made a big cash-paid army **affordable**.

Within his lifetime the system **worked**: the Mongols were repulsed, the Deccan was raided for immense wealth under **Malik Kafur**, and Delhi enjoyed cheap, stable prices. Yet it rested on **fear, espionage and personal supervision**, not on market forces, and it **collapsed soon after his death (1316)** when that iron control lapsed. In an Andhra-linked footnote, it was this very army that overran the **Kakatiyas of Warangal (1310)** and other southern kingdoms. Thus his reforms were a brilliant short-term instrument of centralised power but were **not institutionally sustainable**.
keyPoints: Core aim: maintain a large standing army (against Mongols + Deccan campaigns) without draining the treasury.
Market control: fixed low prices; markets = grain mandi, cloth Sarai Adl, horses/slaves/cattle; supervised by Shahna-i-Mandi.
Diwan-i-Riyasat registered merchants; Barid and munhiyans reported daily; hoarding punished; state grain procurement.
Military: first cash-paid standing army; Dagh (horse-branding) and Chehra (soldier roll) checked fraud.
Interlink: low prices made fixed cash salaries affordable, so a large army was sustainable.
Succeeded in his lifetime (Mongols repelled, Deccan wealth) but collapsed after 1316 as it rested on coercion, not markets.

items.question: "Muhammad-bin-Tughlaq was an ill-fated idealist whose schemes failed in execution rather than conception." Critically discuss.
items.modelAnswer:
Muhammad-bin-Tughlaq (1325–1351) is among the most **debated rulers** of the Delhi Sultanate — a learned, ambitious monarch whose reign is remembered for a cluster of **'failed experiments'**. The verdict that his plans were **sound in idea but flawed in execution** captures much, though not all, of the truth.

His **transfer of the capital from Delhi to Daulatabad (Devagiri)** was strategically reasonable — a central Deccan base to govern the newly won south — but forcing the **whole population** to migrate hundreds of miles caused enormous suffering, and the later reversal wasted resources. His **token currency** of copper coins anticipated the modern idea of fiat money backed by the state, but without control over minting it invited **mass forgery**, and he had to redeem the coins in gold, draining the treasury. The **Doab tax increase** was defensible in principle as a revenue measure, but its timing during **famine** provoked peasant flight and revolt. His planned **Khurasan** and **Qarachil (Himalayan)** expeditions reflected large strategic vision but were **logistically impossible** and abandoned at great cost.

The common thread is a gap between **conception and implementation** — poor timing, inadequate administrative machinery, and a refusal to adapt. Yet the schemes also reveal genuine **administrative imagination**, and his court hosted the traveller **Ibn Battuta**, whose *Rihla* records the era. In the balance, he was neither simply a 'mad' king nor a misunderstood genius, but a ruler whose **idealism outran the capacity of his state** — and whose failures accelerated the **decline of the Sultanate**, opening the way to provincial breakaways and Timur's invasion.
keyPoints: Reputation rests on 'failed experiments': Daulatabad transfer, token currency, Doab tax rise, Khurasan/Qarachil schemes.
Each plan had a rational core — Deccan capital, fiat money, revenue, strategic expansion — but failed in execution.
Daulatabad: sound idea, cruel mass migration and costly reversal; token currency undone by uncontrolled forgery.
Doab tax rise defensible but disastrously timed during famine; Khurasan/Qarachil logistically impossible.
Ibn Battuta's Rihla documents his reign; failures hastened the Sultanate's decline.
Balanced verdict: an idealist whose ambition outran his administrative machinery, not simply a tyrant or a genius.
